title: My Full AI Utilization Project: SumMon ->Divinity 2 (manipulable terrains) + For the King (dice based combat on hex tiles) + Creature Collection
author: NationalGood1065
selftext:
Hello everyone,

As a developer with 10+ years of experience, I started this project in January 2026 to see how far AI technologies had progressed in game development. After nine months of work, it has now reached its current state:

Demo available:  
[https://store.steampowered.com/app/5130400/SumMon/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5130400/SumMon/)

The game is developed in Unity.

For the production pipeline, I used:

Concept Art → GPT Image and NanoBanana  
3D Models → Meshy for model generation, with some model editing done using GPT-6 Astra  
Animations → GPT-6 Astra for rigging and animation generation. It is quite good at rigging, but its animation generation is still average to below average. Instead of making it to generate an animation from scratch, it does better job to retarget animations.

For coding:

System discovery and targeted editing → Gemini  
Gameplay logic implementation → Claude Opus 5.5  
VFX and shaders → Claude Fable 5.1

Before I started coding with AI, I implemented a core architecture called UnCore. It is a fully event-based core with no public functions or variables. All data is managed through DataManager script.

The purpose of this architecture is to constrain the AI as much as possible, forcing it to follow standardized patterns and isolating the technical debt it generates from the rest of the project. This made AI-generated code much more manageable.

Of course, it still requires manual intervention from time to time, but compared to the advantages it provides, I find the trade-off acceptable.

I also used Notion together with AI to generate the GDD based on my own preferences, rules, and design principles. I then applied those rules and parameters directly to Unity through MCP (no reason to use json anymore).

The testing side has also been interesting. I can ask it to generate a complete testing script that compatible with the specific scenario inside the game, makes decisions according to the game's rules and plays through the game automatically. I can then start a testing session, let it play through the entire game, and have it generate a report containing bugs, balancing issues, and problematic sections.

Since my game is turn-based, I also experimented with letting Opus test the game using only image input. It took around two hours to play through approximately 15 minutes of gameplay, but it still managed to provide some interesting and useful feedback. Jev or similar models can be used for testing the game as well I think, but never tested.

Overall, my experience is that game development has changed dramatically. From now on, I think we will be able to create games with much broader scope while requiring less effort.

The key skill is becoming the ability to direct AI in the right direction and position yourself at a higher level of abstraction, rather than focusing only on implementation.

However, current models still have limitations, so you need to carefully choose which level of the development process you delegate to AI and which parts you continue to control manually.

Happy to elaborate any of these topics if asked.
